A model went into production last year. The person who built it has left. Nobody monitors its output. There is no agreed condition under which it gets switched off.

It still runs. It still shapes decisions.

Nobody did anything wrong. That is what makes it hard to find.
Here is how that ends.

In July 2025, a federal court ruled that Workday's HiredScore AI screening features fell within the scope of an ongoing collective action, and directed the parties to set a timeline for Workday to produce the customers that had enabled them.

Workday had argued that HiredScore sat on a separate technology platform and should fall outside the scope. The court disagreed.

The more important ruling had come earlier. The same court held that a screening vendor can potentially act as the employer's agent when the employer delegates traditional hiring functions to it.

That removes the two most comfortable positions in the room.

The employer cannot simply say it is the vendor's problem. The vendor cannot simply say it only makes software.

Now ask the question that matters to you.

Could you produce your own line of that list without asking the vendor?

Not the models your teams built. The AI systems running inside software you bought — screening, scoring, routing, pricing, forecasting, fraud, support.

In many organisations, that list does not exist. Not because someone consciously decided against governance, but because nothing in the delivery process required it.

A model can reach production through the same door as an ordinary feature release. And an ordinary feature release rarely requires a named owner, a retirement condition, and a review cadence.

If you were counting on regulation to force the work, note that the EU has deferred key high-risk obligations for Annex III systems — including recruitment AI — to December 2027.

The date moved. The operational exposure did not.

Three columns is the whole instrument:
→ Name. Every AI system or model influencing a decision in production. Including the ones you bought rather than built.
→ Owner. A person. Not a committee, not a function, not "the platform team."
→ Retirement. The condition under which it gets switched off, and who signs.
Not every model needs the same weight of oversight. A demand forecast is not a hiring decision, and treating them alike is how governance becomes theatre nobody follows.

But the list is not oversight. The list is knowing what you have.

The hardware arrived inside an ownership system. An asset tag, a depreciation schedule, a support contract, and a name on the purchase order.

The model running on it may have arrived outside one.

Infrastructure is not the foundation. It is the part of the foundation that arrives with ownership machinery already attached.

Ever wondered why defense job boards are flooded with unfilled roles, yet qualified professionals get ghosted daily? 

The defense contracting job market operates by a brutal set of rules. Thousands of open positions don't indicate a booming hiring market - they reveal a system choked by structural bottlenecks, rigid compliance, and a stark disconnect in compensation. Here is the hard-hitting truth behind the unfilled numbers:

1. The Strategy of "Ghost Jobs" A massive percentage of open defense listings aren't immediate hires; they are strategic placeholders: The "Proposal Bench": Contractors bidding on massive government contracts must prove they have a workforce before winning the award. They post hundreds of roles to harvest resumes. If they win the bid months later, they call you. If they lose, the job vanishes.

Evergreen Pipelines: Because cleared talent is rare, firms leave high-turnover pipelines open 365 days a year just to stack resumes. Federal rules also force companies to publicly advertise roles they already intend to fill internally.

2. The "Unicorn" Catch-22 Real positions stay empty for months because the entry requirements create an impossible bottleneck: 

The Clearance Trap: Postings require an active Secret or TS/SCI clearance. Companies lose revenue every day a seat sits empty, so they rarely sponsor clean applicants and wait 6–12 months for investigations. Everyone is fighting over the same tiny pool of pre-cleared people. 

Certification Bloat: Under strict mandates like DoD 8140/8570, lacking a specific, rigid certification (like Security+ or CISSP) triggers an automatic ATS rejection - even if the applicant has a decade of elite technical experience.

3. The Unrealistic Salary Range: The biggest bottleneck is the wage disconnect, driven by a rigid floor and a heavily capped ceiling: The Floor ($60k - $80k): Entry-to-mid level roles often require a clean record, a rigid degree, and specific certifications, yet offer low starting wages that fail to compete with local commercial markets. 

The Ceiling ($150k - $180k+ Capped): Contractor pay is structurally capped by fixed government bill rates negotiated years prior. While a cleared professional can make a comfortable living, top-tier software developers, cloud architects, and AI engineers hit a hard ceiling. They can easily command 30% to 50% more in commercial tech - without sacrificing their smartphones, remote flexibility, or privacy to work inside a windowless SCIF. 

The Takeaway: If you're hunting in the defense space, ignore postings older than 14 days. Look for "Immediate Fill" or "Existing Program" and strictly avoid "Contingent upon contract award" unless you're willing to wait months for a job that might never exist.

To my GovCon network: Have you fallen into the "Proposal Bench" trap? Recruiters, how are you overcoming the commercial salary gap?

Hiring is down 24% this year. A handful of roles are barely moving. Almost none of them are technical.

Educators. Lawyers. Architects. Security professionals. That's the short list of jobs holding up while everything around them contracts.

Not because AI can't touch what they do. Because what they do isn't actually the technical part.

I think we've been positioning ourselves wrong for years now, and this is just making it visible faster.

Most senior people I talk to lead with their technical depth when they describe their value. The systems they've built. The frameworks they know cold. The certifications.

None of that is what a client actually remembers about you.

They remember the recommendation you made when the easy answer and the right answer weren't the same thing. They remember that you told them something they didn't want to hear, and you were right.

That judgment call is the part AI can't fully take. Not yet. Maybe not for a long time.

So the actual question for anyone thinking about upskilling right now isn't "which tool should I learn." It's "am I known for my judgment, or just my output." Only one of those survives a hiring freeze.

Something quiet is happening in the numbers.

In the US, Temp Workforce category kept adding jobs for months while permanent hiring stayed soft. Staffing Industry Analysts walked through the Bureau of Labor Statistics print where temp work was rising even as the broader payroll story looked weak. The first July headline made it look like temp was up while total employment fell. Later revisions cleaned that up. 

𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗻𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗯𝘂𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗹𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗯𝘂𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁.

I'm seeing a version of that across APAC too, even if the charts don't look identical.

In India, the Indian Staffing Federation said formal flexi-staffing grew about 8% year on year and added over a hundred thousand workers in twelve months. In Singapore, official stock data still shows most people in permanent roles. But recruiters and surveys keep saying the same thing for 2026: more contract and project hiring, because nobody wants to lock the cost in while the ground is moving.

Why?

Uncertainty. Cost pressure. Money going into AI and transformation while the operating budget stays tight. Roles being redesigned faster than org charts can keep up. When that mix hits, 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗻𝗼𝗻-𝗲𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗼𝘆𝗲𝗲 𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝘂𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗼𝗻. Not because leaders love contingent labour. Because it lets them move without waiting for a headcount committee.

I'm seeing TA and HR roles show up on contracts too. The people who used to only buy flexible labour are sometimes sitting in that same lane themselves.

This isn't a side category anymore. It's how a lot of real work is getting done while companies figure out what stays permanent.

If flexibility is the strategy, someone still has to own the full picture. 𝗪𝗵𝗼'𝘀 𝗼𝗻 𝘄𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗵 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹, 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁𝘀, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗯𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗸𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝘂𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗿.

Six years ago, I had just finished my PhD at 27 years old…and I was babysitting for $20 an hour to pay my bills.

It was August 2020. I had applied to what felt like every full-time research job I could find, gone through interviews, and nothing had worked out. There also weren’t exactly a ton of companies hiring in the middle of COVID.

Then, within my first month of babysitting, a recruiter called me about a four-month contract at Expedia Group 

I said yes.

At the time, I don’t think I even fully realized the role was for a quantitative UX researcher. I definitely didn’t realize that four-month contract would be extended again…and again…eventually turn into a full-time role, and somehow become six years of my career.

And those six years have looked nothing like what I could have predicted.

I came in thinking of myself as a quantitative researcher. Today, much of my work is qualitative. Along the way, I’ve learned entirely new methodologies, experimented with new tools, worked with AI, and researched problems across almost every part of the travel experience.

I’ve worked on everything traveler facing from pricing and fees to lodging, checkout, app retention, referrals, destination discovery, property sharing, flight price tracking, and plenty of things I’m forgetting as I write this.

The biggest thing I’ve learned from working at a large company for six years might actually be adaptability.

Teams change. Priorities change. Products change. The questions we need to answer change. And sometimes the version of your career you imagined for yourself changes too.

At 27, I was very worried that finishing a PhD without a full-time job meant I was somehow behind.

Now, six years later, I think a lot about how little I understood about what was actually happening in that moment.

I thought I was taking a temporary job.

Really, I was stepping into the beginning of a career I could not have planned.

So if there’s one thing I’d tell my 27-year-old self, it’s this: not every good opportunity arrives looking like the big break.

Sometimes it looks like a four-month contract.

Sometimes it looks like a detour.

And sometimes you only realize years later that it was the thing that changed everything.
